newsitem.title: USA: US April NAPM sign of firm growth, low inflation.
newsitem.headline: US April NAPM sign of firm growth, low inflation.

text.p: Signs of slightly slower growth in manufacturing during April painted a picture of continued U.S. economic strength devoid of any concrete evidence of inflation, econmists said.
"It's kind of a microcosm of all the other data we got on the economy, strong real economic activity but still great price performance," said John Williams, chief economist at Bankers Trust Co.
The National Association of Purchasing Management said on Thursday that its lead index fell to 54.2 from 55.0 in March.

The number was above forecasts for a 53.6 April index but economists said the prices index, which fell to 49.6 from 50.9 in March, should put U.S. credit markets in a buoyant mood before Friday's all-important April jobs data.
Economists said auto strikes may have temporarily depressed the manufacturing sector in April. Other components pointed to strong growth after a slight slowing, they said.

The employment index rose to 52.8 in April from 51.6, the highest reading in the current economic cycle, economists said. New orders, at 57.9, were still robust, although under the bubbly 60.3 the previous month.
"All the real economic activity components are very much on the strong side, consistent with the notion that the manufacturing sector is doing just fine, thank you," Williams said.
The NAPM data came one day after a shocking 5.6-percent surge in the advance first quarter gross domestic product reading, fueled in part by a major buildup in inventories.

Thursday's manufacturing data gave the first read on economic activity in the second quarter and analysts said if the index eases further in coming months it could suggest a tamer economy in the April-through-June period.

"If NAPM continues to soften, maybe production will slow, causing inventory gains to slow as well, and economic growth will become more moderate in the second quarter," said Sung Won Sohn, chief economist at Norwest Corp.
"I distinctly feel the economy is slowing, but the pace is still too fast," Sohn said.

The next important snapshot of the current quarter comes on Friday, when the Labor Department releases the April employment report and non-farm payrolls data. The unemployment rate was expected to have held at March's 5.2 percent, and payrolls were seen rising 211,000.
Whether or not the Federal Reserve raises interest rates at the next gathering of policy makers on May 20 could hinge on the employment report.

But economists said if the NAPM index is any guide, the central bank probably has at a least one more snugging of monetary policy in store this year, to ensure inflation does not hitch on the U.S. growth locomotive.

"What this data today tells us is there is a slowing, but it is very slight indeed," said Richard Berner, chief economist at Mellon Bank Corp. "I think the Fed is still on track to tighten on May 20."
